replies:
Great — I'll run a mock interview. First question now:

"Walk me through your resume and tell me why you're a good fit for this financial analyst role."

Answer as you would in the room (spoken, 60–90 seconds). I'll score structure, evidence and specificity, give one concrete improvement, then ask the next question.

Score: 3/10.

Why: your answer is a fragment and too high-level for an interviewer. They asked "Walk me through your resume and tell me why you're a good fit" — they expect a short story of who you are, key achievements with metrics, and one clear tie to the role. Instead you described a technical task (build a three-statement model) with no resume overview, no evidence of impact, no timeline, and no company fit.
One concrete improvement: give a 60–90 second spoken answer with this structure — 1) one-line background (current title, years, main focus), 2) two short accomplishment bullets with numbers (what you did, the result), 3) one sentence connecting those accomplishments to this role and why you want it. Example rewrite you can memorize (fill [brackets]):
"I’m [current title] with [X years] of financial modeling and forecasting experience, most recently at [Company], where I led the quarterly planning model for a $[size] business. I built a three-statement model that improved forecasting accuracy from [Y]% to [Z]% and identified cost reductions that saved $[amount] annually. Before that I supported 10+ M&A diligence projects, building comps and valuations that the deal team used to set bid ranges. Those experiences — building rigorous models, validating them against comps, and turning outputs into clear recommendations — are exactly what this financial analyst role needs, and I’m excited by [one thing about the firm or team you know]."
Next question: do you want me to mock the next interview question now? (default: yes; I’ll ask it).

Score: 5/10.

Why: your reply improved by including a concrete modeling method (three-statement model) and a check against comps, which shows you know relevant technical work. But it still misses the interviewer's request components: no resume overview or background, no accomplishments with metrics or outcomes, no timeline, and no explicit tie to why you're a fit for this specific role or firm. It reads like a technical checklist, not a personal pitch.

One concrete improvement: expand to the three-part structure I gave earlier and add one measurable accomplishment and a sentence about fit. Fill these placeholders with your facts:
"I’m [current title] with [X years] in [finance/industry], most recently at [Company]. I built a three-statement model that [what it changed — improved forecast accuracy, supported a $X decision, saved $Y], and I validated outputs against comps to [result— e.g., refine valuation, adjust guidance]. I also [second accomplishment with metric]. Those skills — rigorous modeling, benchmarking to comps, and turning analysis into recommendations — match this role because [specific reason about the team or firm]."

Want me to score a rewritten answer if you paste one now?

Prep for a final-round analyst interview at Lincoln International — focused, practical, and ready-to-use.
What interviewers at this stage want (short)
- Fit and coachability: evidence you learn fast, take feedback, and sustain long hours.
- Technical competence: clear, correct valuation/accounting reasoning and tidy modeling instincts.
- Deal judgment: quick, structured sense of value drivers, synergies and risks.
- Communication: concise answers, good story structure, and thoughtful questions.
Top question types and exactly how to answer them
1) Walk me through your resume
- Structure: 30–45s past → 30–45s current → 30–45s why Lincoln & this role. Tie each stop to a skill (modeling, diligence, client exposure).
- Quick script: “I started in [role]; there I learned X (modeling/valuation), then moved to [role] where I led Y (tight-deadline models/client work). Most recently I did Z — I want Lincoln for hands-on middle‑market M&A exposure because [one sentence].”
2) Why Lincoln / why this group?
- Say middle‑market focus + cross‑border capability + hands‑on analyst exposure (or cite a recent Lincoln deal if you know one). Then one sentence on how your background maps to their deal flow and what you want to learn.

3) Technical — Walk me through a DCF
- Steps: forecast unlevered free cash flow → discount with WACC → compute terminal value (exit multiple or perpetuity) → sum to enterprise value → subtract net debt for equity value. Call out key assumptions (revenue growth, margins, capex, working capital, terminal method) and sensitivity to WACC/terminal.
4) Technical — Compare valuation methods
- Give three: DCF (best for detailed, company-specific cash flow view), comps (market context, quick check), precedent transactions (control premiums, strategic context). Say when each is preferred and a one-line limitation.

6) Modeling/Excel test
- Narrate inputs → show assumptions → build outputs → sanity-check with margin and growth comparables. Keep model tidy (inputs separate, clearly named outputs) and explain sensitivity runs.

7) Behavioral (conflict, missed deadline)
- Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. End with the lesson and a metric if possible (time saved, error avoided, client retained).
8) Deal judgment/case quick take
- Framework: describe business → key value drivers and margins → market and competition → buyer rationale → high-level valuation range and 2–3 risks/mitigants.

9) Questions to ask them (pick 3)
- “What’s a typical week for a first-year analyst on live deals?”
- “Can you tell me about a recent deal the team did and what made it challenging?”
- “What skills separate analysts who get promoted here?”
Two short model answers you can memorize
- DCF: “A DCF projects unlevered free cash flow for a forecast period, discounts at WACC, adds a terminal value (I’d use an exit multiple if peer M&A activity supports it), sums to enterprise value and subtracts net debt for equity value. Sensitivities: terminal growth and WACC.”
- Behavioral (team disagreement): “Situation: teammate pushed for aggressive revenue assumptions on a live model. Task: ensure realistic forecast. Action: I built conservative and base sensitivity cases and showed sector comps and customer contract data. Result: we adopted a blended case, client accepted it, and the model held through diligence. I learned to pair data with options, not confrontation.”
10-point day-before / day-of checklist
1. Re-read job description and group focus; note 1–2 sector examples they cover.
2. Print/have resume open; mark 2–3 STAR stories tied to modeling, deadlines and client exposure.
3. Run through 3 core technical rehearsals: DCF walkthrough, comps vs precedent rationale, and an accounting linkage.
4. Open Excel and practice a 5-minute sensitivity table and narrate what you’d say about results.
5. Prepare 3 tailored questions per interviewer.
6. Have concise closing line ready: why you, why them, what you’ll bring.
7. Check interview tech/route (Zoom link, camera, mic, backups).
8. Prepare one-page notes: bullet DCF steps, comps logic, 3 deal frameworks, and your [your skill] prompts.
9. Sleep, hydrate, and eat beforehand.
10. Plan a short email or thank-you note to send within 24 hours (I can draft it).

Common pitfalls to avoid
- Over‑long answers without structure; use 1–3 chunks.
- Guessing numbers without stating assumptions.
- Vague claims about your role on deals—be specific about what you did.

Mock question to practice now
- “Tell me about a recent M&A deal you followed. What made it attractive and what were the risks?” Type your answer here and I’ll score it for structure, evidence and specificity and give one concrete fix, then ask the next question.

You don't have any applications or postings on file yet. The one step that starts this is: pick the first job posting for me to prepare (paste its link or tell me the company and exact role) or say "search for [role] in [city]" and I'll find matches.

When you pick the first posting, here is exactly what I will put on the application card for that posting — every field the employer will see or the Trainee extension will ask you to confirm before anything is sent. I list each field and what I will fill or leave for you to type:
1) Employer and job
- Company: exactly as the posting shows.
- Job title: exactly as the posting shows.
- Location: the posting's location (city / remote / on-site / hybrid and any site-specific detail).

2) Applicant contact header (what appears at the top of your resume and application)
- Full name: blank until you type or confirm it; I will not guess.
- Email: blank until you type or confirm it; I will not guess.
- Phone: blank until you type or confirm it; I will not guess.
- LinkedIn / portfolio URL: included only if you provide or confirm one.
3) Resume file
- File attached: I will use the tailored PDF I create only from your confirmed facts, or the resume file you upload if you prefer.
- Resume filename: suggested like "YourName Company Role.pdf" but you can change it.
- Notes shown: which confirmed facts are included (job titles, dates, schools) so you can verify truth.
4) Cover letter / application text
- Cover letter (optional): I will draft a 100–120 word letter tailored to the posting with [brackets] for any missing specifics (hiring manager name, exact start date, a named referral).
- Employer-specific long-answer fields or essay boxes: I will draft concise answers from your confirmed facts and the posting text; anything missing will be left blank for you to complete.
5) Screening questions (yes/no, multiple choice, or short text)
- For each posted screening question I will:
  - Show the question.
  - Pre-fill an answer only from confirmed facts (work authorization, years of experience, visa status, salary expectation, willingness to relocate, etc.). If you haven't confirmed the relevant fact, the field stays blank for you.
  - Flag any question that could disqualify you so you can edit it.

6) Additional attachments
- Portfolio, code samples, transcripts, references: each listed and attached only if you uploaded them or I have a confirmed fact linking them. Otherwise the card will show these slots empty.
7) Work authorization / visa status
- Field: pre-filled only if you previously confirmed it; otherwise blank and required before sending.

8) Salary / compensation expectation
- Field: left blank unless you tell me the number you want included; I will not invent a pay number. If the posting requests a range, I will show how the posting's stated pay compares (if the posting listed pay).

9) Availability / earliest start date
- Field: left blank unless you confirm an exact date; I will suggest a phrasing like "Available [month/day/year]" if you give the date.
10) Custom recruiter-screen fields
- For any custom field on the employer's form (e.g., "Describe your experience with X tool" or "How many years in Y industry"):
  - I will draft concise, truthful answers using only confirmed facts; if a needed fact isn't on file, that answer will be blank for you to write or confirm.

11) Consent / policy checkboxes
- Privacy/consent checkboxes will be shown for you to check; I will not check them for you.

12) Referral / employee connection fields
- "Referred by" or similar: left blank unless you supply a contact name and their employer.
13) Application note to recruiter (optional)
- Short note (1–2 lines): I will draft an optional line such as "Happy to discuss how my [skill] at [former employer] maps to this role" with brackets for any missing detail.

14) Submission metadata (for your tracking)
- Resume version used, cover letter version, time prepared, and which confirmed facts were included — all recorded on the card so you can review exactly what will be sent.
What I will not do on this card without your explicit approval
- I will not click "submit" or send the application. After the card is prepared, you will review every field in the Trainee extension and approve sending.
- I will not invent or confirm profile facts for you. Any draft facts used will be shown as drafts and must be confirmed by you before they are used in the resume or answers.
- I will not fill your name, email, phone, work authorization, or pay expectation without your explicit text in this chat.
One-step next: paste the job link or tell me Company + exact job title (or say "search for X in Y") so I can read the posting and prepare that card. Is that the one you want me to prepare first?
